description: RAM, ROM, flash and virtual memory; magnetic, optical, solid-state and cloud storage explained.
content_html:
Why Computers Need Different Types of Storage

No single storage technology can do everything well. The storage inside a computer is organised into a hierarchy: the fastest storage sits closest to the CPU (registers, then cache), but it is tiny and expensive. Cheaper, larger storage sits further away but takes longer to access. Understanding where each type fits — and why — is essential for your exam.

Storage falls into two broad categories. Primary storage is directly accessible by the CPU: it includes RAM, ROM, cache and flash memory. Secondary storage is not directly accessible by the CPU; files must be loaded into primary storage before the CPU can work with them.

RAM — Random Access Memory

RAM is the computer’s main working memory. Everything the CPU is actively using — the operating system, open applications, files being edited — is held in RAM. RAM is volatile: it loses all its contents when power is removed. It is also read/write: the CPU can both read from it and write to it during normal operation.

The more RAM a computer has, the more programs it can keep open simultaneously without slowing down. A typical modern desktop might have 8 GB to 32 GB of RAM. RAM connects to the CPU via the memory bus; access time is around 50–100 nanoseconds, much slower than cache but far faster than any secondary storage device.

ROM — Read-Only Memory

ROM is non-volatile — it keeps its contents when the power is off. As its name suggests, it is read-only under normal operation: the CPU can read from it but cannot change its contents during normal use. ROM holds firmware such as the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System), which runs first when a computer starts, checking hardware and loading the operating system from secondary storage.

Because ROM retains data without power, it is ideal for storing start-up instructions. Without ROM, a computer would not know how to begin loading the operating system after being switched on.

Flash Memory and Virtual Memory

Flash memory is a form of non-volatile storage that can be both read from and written to without requiring power to retain its data. USB flash drives, SD cards, smartphones and solid-state drives all use flash memory. Because it has no moving parts, it is more durable than magnetic hard drives and faster to access.

Virtual memory is not a physical component but a technique. When RAM fills up, the operating system moves the least-recently-used sections of RAM to a reserved area on the secondary storage device (a ‘page file’ or ‘swap space’). This frees up RAM for the task currently in use. The downside is significant: secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so heavy use of virtual memory causes the system to slow dramatically — a problem called thrashing.

Key Fact

Volatile (loses data without power): RAM, cache. Non-volatile (retains data without power): ROM, flash memory, all secondary storage devices. Virtual memory uses secondary storage, so it is non-volatile, but using it is slow.

Secondary Storage — The Four Types

Secondary storage provides permanent, high-capacity storage for files, programs and data. There are four types you must be able to compare on five criteria: capacity, durability, portability, speed and cost.

Magnetic Storage (HDD)

Magnetic hard disk drives (HDDs) store data as tiny magnetised regions on spinning metal platters. A moving read/write head swings over the platter surface to read or write data. HDDs offer very high capacity (up to several TB for consumer drives) at a relatively low cost per gigabyte. However, the mechanical moving parts make them slower than solid-state alternatives and more vulnerable to physical shock.

Solid-State Storage (SSD)

Solid-state drives (SSDs) use the same flash memory technology as USB drives, but in a larger, faster form. Because there are no moving parts, SSDs access data much faster than HDDs (access times measured in microseconds rather than milliseconds), are silent, run cooler, and withstand knocks and drops far better. The trade-off is cost: SSDs cost significantly more per gigabyte than HDDs, though the gap has narrowed in recent years.

Optical Storage

Optical storage uses a laser to read (and sometimes write) data encoded on a disc surface. CDs hold around 700 MB, DVDs 4.7 GB (or 8.5 GB dual-layer) and Blu-ray discs up to 50 GB. Optical media is highly portable and cheap per disc, but access speed is slow compared to SSDs and HDDs, and discs can be scratched, making them less durable for frequent daily use.

Cloud Storage

Cloud storage stores files on remote servers accessed via the internet, such as Google Drive, OneDrive or iCloud. From the user’s perspective, files are available on any internet-connected device anywhere in the world. Capacity is theoretically unlimited (you simply pay for more storage). However, access speed depends on the internet connection, and there are concerns about security (files held by a third party) and privacy (who can access the data). If the internet connection fails, files may be temporarily inaccessible.

Key Fact

Comparison summary: SSDs are faster and more durable than HDDs but more expensive per GB. HDDs offer higher capacity per pound. Optical media is cheap and portable but slow and scratchable. Cloud storage is accessible anywhere but needs internet and raises security concerns.

The table below compares the four secondary storage types on the five criteria your exam uses:

CriterionHDD (Magnetic)SSD (Solid-State)Optical (DVD)Cloud
CapacityVery high (multi-TB)High (2 TB+)Low (4.7 GB)Effectively unlimited
DurabilityFragile (moving parts)Very durable (no moving parts)Can be scratchedHigh (server-side redundancy)
PortabilityModerate (heavy)Good (light)High (small disc)Very high (any device, anywhere)
SpeedModerate (~100 MB/s)Fast (~500 MB/s+)Slow (~10 MB/s)Depends on internet speed
CostLow per GBHigher per GBVery low per discSubscription-based

This exam uses base-2 prefixes for storage calculations. This is critical because answers using base-10 are marked as incorrect on calculation questions:

  • 1 KB (kilobyte) = \(2^{10}\) = 1,024 bytes
  • 1 MB (megabyte) = \(2^{20}\) = 1,048,576 bytes
  • 1 GB (gigabyte) = \(2^{30}\) = 1,073,741,824 bytes

For image storage calculations: multiply width (pixels) × height (pixels) × bit depth (bits per pixel). This gives the total in bits. Divide by 8 to get bytes, then divide by 1,024 repeatedly for KB, MB, GB. Forgetting to divide by 8 at the first step is the most common error.
exam_tip_html: Compare questions about storage require you to contrast two types explicitly against each named criterion — do not just list features of each separately. For example: “Unlike an HDD, which uses spinning platters and can be damaged by physical shock, an SSD has no moving parts and is therefore more durable.” That is one comparison point worth 1 mark. For storage calculation questions, always use base-2 prefixes (1 KB = 1,024 bytes) and show each conversion step: multiply pixel dimensions by bit depth for bits, divide by 8 for bytes, divide by 1,024 for KB, divide again for MB.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary storage (RAM, ROM, cache, flash) is directly accessible by the CPU. RAM is volatile and read/write; ROM is non-volatile and read-only. Flash memory is non-volatile and rewritable.
  • Virtual memory uses secondary storage as an overflow area when RAM is full, but is far slower and causes performance problems if overused.
  • Secondary storage types — magnetic (HDD), solid-state (SSD), optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray) and cloud — are compared on five criteria: capacity, durability, portability, speed and cost. SSDs are fastest and most durable; HDDs offer the most capacity per pound; optical is cheap and portable; cloud requires internet but is accessible anywhere.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a characteristic of RAM?
A) Non-volatile and read-only
B) Volatile and read/write
C) Non-volatile and read/write
D) Volatile and read-only
State one advantage of an SSD over an HDD.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: faster access speed / more durable (no moving parts) / silent in operation / lower power consumption. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A digital photograph is 4,000 pixels wide and 3,000 pixels tall. Each pixel is stored using 24 bits. Calculate the storage required for this image in megabytes (MB). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Step 1: 4,000 × 3,000 × 24 = 288,000,000 bits [1 mark]
Step 2: 288,000,000 ÷ 8 = 36,000,000 bytes [1 mark]
Step 3: 36,000,000 ÷ 1,024 ÷ 1,024 = approximately 34.3 MB [1 mark for correct final answer in MB using base-2]
Note: answers using base-10 (36,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 36 MB) do not receive the unit-conversion mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of virtual memory and describe one disadvantage of using it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Virtual memory is a section of secondary storage used as an extension of RAM when physical RAM is full. [1 mark]
• The operating system moves sections of RAM that have not been recently used to the secondary storage page file, freeing RAM for the currently active task. [1 mark]
• Disadvantage: secondary storage (e.g. HDD or SSD) is much slower than RAM, so relying on virtual memory causes a noticeable slowdown in system performance. [1 mark]
• Additional relevant point, e.g. if virtual memory is used heavily it can cause 'thrashing' — the OS spends more time swapping data than running programs. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare magnetic hard disk drives (HDDs) with solid-state drives (SSDs) using the criteria: speed, durability and cost.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (2 marks per criterion — 1 for each storage type, with an explicit contrast):
Speed: SSDs are significantly faster than HDDs because they use flash memory with no moving parts; HDDs rely on a spinning platter and moving read/write head, introducing mechanical delay (seek time and rotational latency).
Durability: SSDs are more durable because they have no mechanical components that can break or wear out; HDDs contain spinning platters and moving heads that can be damaged by physical shock.
Cost: HDDs are cheaper per gigabyte than SSDs and are therefore preferred when large capacity storage is needed at low cost; SSDs cost more per GB but the price gap has narrowed.
Mastering: All three criteria addressed with clear, explicit contrasts and precise technical vocabulary.
Secure: Two or three criteria addressed with clear contrasts but limited technical detail.
Developing: One or two criteria compared, but contrasts implied rather than explicit.
Emerging: Features of one storage type listed without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of cloud storage compared to local secondary storage for a student storing their school work. Consider at least three criteria in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of cloud storage:
• Accessible from any internet-connected device — allows the student to work at home, school and on mobile devices without carrying physical media.
• Effectively unlimited capacity (subscription-based), removing worry about running out of space.
• Files are backed up on remote servers with redundancy, so local hardware failure does not cause data loss.
• Easy to share files with teachers or group members.
Disadvantages of cloud storage:
• Requires a reliable internet connection — files may be inaccessible without internet.
• Security and privacy concerns: files are held by a third party who may be subject to data breaches.
• Ongoing cost: subscription fees apply for large storage quotas.
• Slower access speed than a local SSD if internet bandwidth is limited.
Mastering: Balanced discussion of at least three criteria with explicit advantages AND disadvantages, anchored to the context (student), and a reasoned concluding judgement.
Secure: Three criteria discussed with advantages and disadvantages, but judgement is limited.
Developing: Two criteria discussed; one-sided or limited in context relevance.
Emerging: A list of points without development or explicit criteria.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of primary storage holds the BIOS firmware and retains its contents without power?
Which secondary storage type is most likely to be damaged by physical shock?
Virtual memory uses a section of _____ storage as an overflow area when RAM is full.
RAM is described as _____ because it loses its contents when power is removed.
Match each storage type to its key characteristic:
right: Fast, no moving parts, uses flash memory
Mechanical platters, cheaper per GB, slower

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'volatile' mean when describing storage?
flashcard_questions.a: Data is lost when power is removed.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of volatile primary storage.
Give one example of non-volatile primary storage.
What type of instructions does ROM typically hold?
flashcard_questions.a: Firmware such as the BIOS, which starts the computer.
Non-volatile memory that can be electrically erased and reprogrammed, used in SSDs and USB drives.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is virtual memory slower than RAM?
flashcard_questions.a: It uses secondary storage (e.g. HDD or SSD), which is much slower than RAM.

flashcard_questions.q: How does an SSD store data differently from an HDD?
flashcard_questions.a: SSD uses flash memory chips with no moving parts; HDD uses spinning magnetic platters.

flashcard_questions.q: Which secondary storage type typically has the highest capacity per pound spent?
flashcard_questions.a: Magnetic HDD — it offers the most gigabytes per pound compared to SSDs.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one advantage of optical storage over HDD.
flashcard_questions.a: Highly portable and very cheap per disc.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one disadvantage of cloud storage compared to local storage.
flashcard_questions.a: Requires an internet connection; inaccessible if offline.

flashcard_questions.q: In base-2, how many bytes are in 1 KB?
A student forgets to divide by 8 in a storage calculation. What error have they made?
flashcard_questions.a: They calculated the size in bits but should have converted to bytes by dividing by 8.

glossary_terms.definition: Storage directly accessible by the CPU without going through input/output channels, including RAM, ROM, cache and flash memory.
Persistent storage not directly accessible by the CPU, used to store files, programs and data long-term, including HDDs, SSDs, optical discs and cloud storage.
Volatile read/write primary storage that holds the operating system, currently running programs and their data.
Non-volatile primary storage that retains its contents without power, typically holding firmware such as the BIOS.
A type of non-volatile memory that can be electrically erased and reprogrammed, used in USB drives, SSDs and smartphones.
A section of secondary storage used by the operating system as an extension of RAM when physical RAM is full.
A secondary storage device that stores data as magnetic patterns on a rotating metal platter, read by a moving read/write head.
A secondary storage device that uses flash memory chips with no moving parts, offering faster access and greater durability than an HDD.
A secondary storage medium that uses a laser to read or write data encoded as pits and lands on the surface of a disc (CD, DVD, Blu-ray).
